Medical knowledge includes morphine poisoning and sleeping sickness but limited understanding
Communication and travel limited to horse-drawn carriages, early railways, and telegrams
location: London, specifically New Inn and Kennington Lane
crime_subtype: chronic poisoning and impersonation to forge a will

cast.private_secret: John Blackmore in disguise, administering poison

cast.name: John Blackmore

cast.alibi_window: present at secret house and elsewhere in disguise

surface_summary: A mysterious patient suffering from morphine poisoning is secretly confined while his brother impersonates him to execute a forged will. The victim's death appears natural or suicidal, but suspicions arise about foul play and forgery. The investigation uncovers a complex scheme of impersonation, chronic poisoning, and deception.
accepted_facts: Jeffrey Blackmore executed a second will that favored his brother John Blackmore
Jeffrey Blackmore was found dead in his chambers at New Inn
A mysterious patient named Mr. Graves was suffering from morphine poisoning
Mr. H. Weiss was involved in secretive and suspicious activities related to Mr. Graves
inferred_conclusions: The second will was genuine and executed by Jeffrey Blackmore himself
Mr. Graves and Jeffrey Blackmore were different persons with no connection
Mr. Weiss was an innocent caretaker concerned for Mr. Graves
mechanism_description: John Blackmore impersonated his brother Jeffrey at New Inn while Jeffrey was secretly confined and chronically poisoned at another location. John forged the second will to benefit himself and murdered Jeffrey by administering morphine poisoning over time. The accomplice Mrs. Schallibaum aided in the deception and disguise, including the use of peculiar spectacles and controlled squint to avoid identification.
delivery_path: John Blackmore assumes the identity of Jeffrey Blackmore at New Inn
Jeffrey Blackmore is secretly confined and chronically poisoned with morphine
John Blackmore forges a second will favoring himself as executor and residuary legatee
Mr. H. Weiss acts as John Blackmore's disguise and accomplice, using peculiar spectacles
Mrs. Schallibaum assists in concealment and surveillance, employing a controllable squint
The victim's death is staged as suicide with the body found at New Inn
The forged will is presented as genuine, supported by false witnesses and signatures
outcome_result: John Blackmore and his accomplices are exposed as the forgers and murderers, and the forged will is invalidated.

false_assumption.statement: The second will was genuine and executed by Jeffrey Blackmore himself in the presence of witnesses.
false_assumption.why_it_seems_reasonable: The will was signed and witnessed by two men who swore to its authenticity and recognized the signatures and finger-marks. The body found was identified as Jeffrey Blackmore, supporting the assumption.
false_assumption.what_it_hides: It hides the fact that the person who signed the will was an impersonator, John Blackmore, and that Jeffrey was secretly confined and poisoned elsewhere.

supporting_points: He administered morphine to Mr. Graves
He used a closed carriage to conceal the patient's location
He had a motive to protect the patient
false_solution.the_one_flaw: He was actually John Blackmore in disguise, and the true culprit behind the murder and forgery.

red_herrings.description: Mrs. Schallibaum's controllable squint suggested she was disguising her identity.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: Her squint was a natural condition she could control voluntarily.

red_herrings.description: The patient's symptoms were initially suspected to be sleeping sickness.
red_herrings.innocent_explanation: The symptoms were actually due to morphine poisoning, not sleeping sickness.

closed_circle.rationale: Only these three had access to the patient and means to administer poison; others were either absent or lacked opportunity.

time_anchors: Twelfth of November last year (second will execution)
Fourteenth of March (Jeffrey Blackmore last seen alive)
Fifteenth of March (Jeffrey Blackmore's body found)
Dates of compass bearings during carriage rides
time_windows: Period between November and March for chronic poisoning
Night of fourteenth to fifteenth March for murder
Visits of Dr. Jervis to secret house
authority_sources: Medical experts Dr. Jervis and John Thorndyke

inference_path.observation: The cuneiform inscription photograph was hung upside down in Jeffrey Blackmore's chambers.
inference_path.correction: The tenant of the chambers was not Jeffrey Blackmore but an impersonator.
inference_path.effect: Raises suspicion that the will signed there may be forged.
required_evidence: Photograph of the cuneiform inscription in the chambers
Testimony of Stephen Blackmore about his uncle's expertise

inference_path.observation: The patient Mr. Graves had symptoms of morphine poisoning and a tremulous iris in the right eye.
inference_path.correction: Mr. Graves is identified as Jeffrey Blackmore, who was secretly confined and poisoned.
inference_path.effect: Establishes identity of victim and suggests foul play.
required_evidence: Medical examination notes by Dr. Jervis
Optician's and oculist's letters describing Jeffrey's spectacles and eye condition

inference_path.observation: The signatures on cheques and wills show abrupt changes but consistent personal character.
inference_path.correction: The changes correspond to intermittent opium use and possible forgery by a relative.
inference_path.effect: Supports theory of impersonation and forgery by John Blackmore.
required_evidence: Expert opinion by bank partner Mr. Britton

inference_path.observation: Pieces of peculiar spectacles and Japanese brush found in New Inn chambers.
inference_path.correction: These items link John Blackmore (tenant of New Inn) and Mr. Weiss (disguised identity).
inference_path.effect: Supports that Weiss and John Blackmore are the same person.
required_evidence: Fragments of spectacles recovered from New Inn
Description of Mr. Weiss's spectacles by Dr. Jervis

inference_path.observation: Cabman Wilkins testifies to a man and woman arriving at New Inn on the night of Jeffrey's death.
inference_path.correction: The woman was Jeffrey Blackmore disguised, the man was John Blackmore impersonating Jeffrey.
inference_path.effect: Explains presence of two persons and supports impersonation theory.
required_evidence: Signed statement of cabman Samuel Wilkins
Description of the woman and man by Wilkins

inference_path.observation: Lump of sugar in tea contained aconitine poison.
inference_path.correction: Mrs. Schallibaum attempted to poison Dr. Jervis to prevent investigation.
inference_path.effect: Confirms active criminal intent and danger to investigators.
required_evidence: Chemical analysis of lump of sugar
Observation of Mrs. Schallibaum's behavior in tea shop

inference_path.observation: John Blackmore and Mr. Weiss never seen together; both have similar disguises and spectacles.
inference_path.correction: They are the same person using disguise to impersonate Jeffrey Blackmore.
inference_path.effect: Identifies the main culprit and explains the deception.
required_evidence: Witness observations of Mr. Weiss and coachman

discriminating_test.design: Recreate the carriage journey using the compass and timing method to locate the secret house precisely. Then gain access to the house and observe the presence of massive bolts, concealed windows, and other security measures. Compare the spectacles fragments with known prescriptions to identify the wearer. Finally, test the sugar lump for poison to confirm the attempt on Dr. Jervis.
discriminating_test.knowledge_revealed: This test confirms the exact location of the secret house, the imprisonment of Jeffrey Blackmore, the disguise and identity of John Blackmore as Mr. Weiss, and the criminal poisoning attempts.
discriminating_test.pass_condition: The secret house is located at the precise coordinates from the compass notes, the spectacles match the unique prescription of Jeffrey Blackmore, and the sugar contains aconitine poison.

fair_play_explanation: The reader is provided with detailed observations, compass notes, witness statements, and descriptions of the spectacles and signatures. The peculiarities of the spectacles and the inverted inscription are highlighted. The suspicious behavior of Mr. Weiss and Mrs. Schallibaum, as well as the cabman testimonies, are all presented openly. The reader could deduce the impersonation and poisoning scheme by connecting these clues.
